# Chaddantajātaka (Ja 514)

**ID:** Ja 514
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Chaddantajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Six-Tusked Elephant
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja514

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Chaddantajātaka* (Ja 514), translated as "The Six-Tusked Elephant," is a narrative preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral; Ohnuma 1997]. Within the canonical narrative frame, the Buddha relates this story at Jetavana regarding a female novice [SuttaCentral]. The core tale recounts the Bodhisatta's previous birth as Chaddanta, a majestic elephant endowed with six tusks emitting multicolored light, who reigns over a herd of eight thousand elephants [Ohnuma 1997; Ohnuma, Head, Eyes]. Offended by a perceived slight, one of his two queen consorts starves herself after vowing to avenge herself in her next birth [Wood 2005; Murphy]. Reborn as Queen Subhaddā, she dispatches the hunter Soṇuttara—dressed in ascetic robes—to secure the elephant's tusks [Ohnuma 2007; Ohnuma 1997; Ohnuma, Head, Eyes]. When the hunter struggles to remove them, the wounded Bodhisatta assists by grasping the saw with his trunk to sever his own tusks, after which his body is ceremonially cremated as five hundred paccekabuddhas recite texts [Ohnuma 2007; Ohnuma, Head, Eyes].

Celebrated by Léon Feer as "un véritable drame" on account of its emotional pathos and dramatic dialogues [Winternitz 1933; Nariman 1919], the story stands as a classic embodiment of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*) through physical self-sacrifice [Ohnuma 2007; Jory 2016]. The narrative exerted a lasting impact on visual and vernacular culture across Buddhist Asia, appearing on the gateways of Sāñcī, in the murals of Ajantā, on *sīmā* boundary stones on the Khorat Plateau, and in Southeast Asian literary compositions such as mid-twentieth-century Khmer poetic laments [Shyu 2008; Murphy; Walker].

SuttaCentral notes verse parallels between Ja 514 and verses in the *Dhammapada* (Dhp 9–10), the *Kāsāvajātaka* (Ja 221), the *Phussattheragāthā* (Thag 17.1), the Gāndhārī Dharmapada (G-Dhp 182–200), the Patna Dharmapada (P-Dhp 84–95), Udānavarga recensions (UV 29), and Chinese translations (T 210, T 212, T 213), as well as references in the *Milindapañha* [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus matches confirm Pali-internal reuse with the *Dhammapada* (specifically Dhp 9–10) and comprehensive alignment with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns the text with northern Buddhist literature, including the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* and the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, as well as Tibetan translations of Haribhaṭṭa's *Jātakamālā* and the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* [DharmaNexus], paralleling related transmissions preserved in Kang Senghui's *Liudu ji jing* and Aśvaghoṣa's *Sūtrālaṅkāra* [Trung Huynh 2016; Ohnuma 1997].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for Ja 514 — Supplied canonical framework, English title, parallels across early Buddhist corpora, and Milindapañha citation.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus match data for Ja 514 — Identified Pali internal reuse with the Dhammapada and Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, and cross-language alignments in Sanskrit and Tibetan.
- [Wood 2005] Leela Aditi Wood, Buddha and the Shape of Belief: Indic Visual Jatakamalas (2005) — Described the Bodhisatta's worship of paccekabuddhas and the consort's revenge vow.

- [Ohnuma 2007] Reiko Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh and Blood: Giving Away the Body in Indian Buddhist Literature (2007) — Analyzed the narrative role of Queen Subhaddā and the hunter Soṇuttara in bodily gift-giving.
- [Ohnuma, Head, Eyes] Reiko Ohnuma, Head, Eyes, Flesh, and Blood: The Body in Buddhist Literature — Detailed the elephant's magical tusks, the self-severing of the tusks with a saw, and the cremation attended by paccekabuddhas.
- [Ohnuma 1997] Reiko Ohnuma, De donis: The Gift of the Body in Indian Buddhist Narrative Literature (Ph.D. dissertation, 1997) — Provided textual synopsis of Ja 514 and related avadāna versions such as Aśvaghoṣa's Sūtrālaṅkāra.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Cited Léon Feer's evaluation of the Jātaka as a true drama.
- [Nariman 1919] G. K. Nariman, Literary History of Sanskrit Buddhism (1919) — Discussed the dramatic ballad nature of the Chaddanta Jātaka.
- [Jory 2016] Patrick Jory, Thailand’s Theory of Monarchy (2016) — Discussed the central position of the Chaddanta Jātaka in the perfection of giving.
- [Walker] Trent Walker, Unfolding Buddhism: Communal Scripts, Localized Translations, and the Work of the Dying in Cambodian Chanted Leporellos — Cited the twentieth-century Khmer verse lament of Chaddanta.
